translation:
Speaking further of these hidden thieves: knowing the names of these seven thieves is astonishing to everyone, and on hearing their names it might seem that whoever calls such pillars of devotion "thieves" has himself gone astray. But all of them have infiltrated in such a way that everyone takes these thieves to be the very ones granting true devotion — which is exactly why Jivandasji Maharaj calls them shahukar chor ("respectable thief" — a thief who is trusted like an honest merchant). The reasons for this have been shown in the discussion within the satsang (holy gathering/discourse), and at the very end of the satsang their full reckoning has been given. So let us now consider why each of these has been called a thief.

First:

The Ten Avatars — this has been discussed in the Prabodh Anga (chapter), and it is also mentioned in the satsang while discussing the story of Ambarish.

_dash avatarke dagdage | bhulya sab sansar ||
ko ek ugare jivana | jine gurumukh kiyo vichar ||34||_ (Deluded by the flicker of the ten avatars, the whole world has gone astray. Only some rare one is saved, O Jivana, who has reflected through the guru's teaching.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says: because God took on the ten avatars in the episode of Ambarish, all the people of the world fell into doubt about devotion to God; but those devotees who had received true understanding from their guru — some rare one among them — were saved from this.

In the satsang, in the chapter on Morli Manohar Parmeshwar (the flute-charming Lord), it is stated that Durvasa's curse was upon Ambarish, and to avert that curse, God agreed to take on the ten avatars in place of Ambarish. So the ten avatars are only names of the forms God assumed; but the God-essence (bhagavat-tattva) that agreed to take the ten avatars is God's original, true form. Therefore it is the Parbrahma God-essence itself, in name and form, that should be worshipped. The names that arose from the forms God took are, as name-forms, illusory (mithya); but the essential Name-Form remains unbroken and eternal.

_avatar aparadhi kahe jivana | jake nahi guru pir ||
aadi ant madhya shamlo | nirgun brahma sharir ||35||_ (Only the sinful offenders, O Jivana, who have no true guru, count God among the avatars. He who is the dark-hued Shyam is present at the beginning, middle, and end — his body is that of the formless, attributeless Brahma.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says: it is only those sinful offenders whose guru is not capable who count God among the avatars. But God, who is Parbrahma, beyond the three gunas (qualities of nature), is Himself present before the avatars, after them, and during them as well — and throughout, He was one and the same, the dark-hued Krishna.

_ram krishna je jivana | do sargun avatar ||
andh dhandh kaha bhaju | je ved na pave paak ||36||_ (Ram and Krishna, O Jivana, are the two avatars with attributes (saguna). Why worship blindly in confusion, when even the Vedas cannot fathom them fully?)

Jivandasji Maharaj says: Ram and Krishna are the two saguna (with-attribute) avatars of Parbrahma. But even the Veda-Brahma cannot understand this saguna-nirguna essence — so what need is there to fall into confusion over the saguna-nirguna question regarding Ram and Krishna, who are beyond all attributes (gunatit)?

By this sakhi (couplet), Ram and Krishna are counted among the ten avatars — but that avatar-form of Ram and Krishna is only a glimpse of God's saguna avatar. Indeed, Ram and Krishna are a glimpse of God's saguna avatar; yet Ram and Krishna, both before and after the avatar and even now, remain unbroken in name-form.

_kab raghupati kab jadupati | do sagun avatar ||
bemukh na samajh jivana | ai sab ekakar ||38||_ (Sometimes as Raghupati [Ram, lord of the Raghu clan], sometimes as Jadupati [Krishna, lord of the Yadu clan] — these are the two saguna avatars. Those who are turned away [faithless] do not understand, O Jivana, that all these are one and the same.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says: sometimes as Ram and sometimes as Krishna, God takes avatar for the welfare of devotees, but those without this understanding fail to grasp that both these forms belong to the one and same Supreme God.

_dase avatare shamlo | chovise akhand ||
sab sakhiyanma jivana | vyapyo kot brahmand ||38||_ (The dark-hued Lord is present, whole and undivided, in all ten avatars as well as in all twenty-four avatars. He pervades all the gopis, O Jivana, and pervades crores of universes as well.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says: Lord Krishna is contained, undivided, in all ten avatars as well as in the twenty-four avatars. That same Krishna pervades all the gopis, and in the same way pervades crores of universes. The God who pervades crores of universes also pervades in the midst of the gopis.

In Krishnadas's Parchari, it is said regarding the avatars of Ram and Krishna:

_ram krishna e puran brahma | ja samarte mite sab karma ||492||
ehi anjan mahe arup | ehi chaud lokko bhuya ||493||_ (Ram and Krishna are the complete Brahma; remembering them erases all karma. They, though within maya, are formless; they are the lords of the fourteen worlds.)

Ram and Krishna are the complete Brahma, the Supreme God. By remembering and worshipping them, all karmic faults and sins are removed. They themselves are the formless Supreme God within saguna maya. Such are they — the ruler-owners of the fourteen worlds.

_ehi sakal srishtike karta | pratipalan sabke harta ||494||
arup anjanme avinashi | avadhpuri vrindavan vasi ||495||_ (They are the creators of all creation, the sustainers and also the destroyers of all. Formless and imperishable within maya, they dwell in Avadhpuri [Ayodhya] and Vrindavan.)

They themselves are the creators of the entire world, the all-powerful ones who nurture and sustain all, and who also destroy all. Formless and imperishable even within saguna maya, they are the very manifest God who resides in Ayodhya and Vrindavan.

Sakhi (couplet):

_kabir ramkrishna avatar kahe | man dhave chatu aur ||
so aparadhi jivku | chaud lok nahi thaur ||46||417||_ (Kabir says: those who call Ram and Krishna mere avatars, whose mind keeps running elsewhere — such offending souls find no place anywhere in the fourteen worlds.)

Das Kabirji says: those who say that Ram and Krishna came by taking avatar, and who keep letting their minds run astray in every direction — such sinful souls will find no salvation anywhere among the fourteen worlds. They will meet with downfall.

Thus Jivandasji, citing Krishnadas as well, has called the ten avatars a shahukar chor (respectable thief).

In Handwritten Manuscript No. 48, page 49, in the 20th verse of "Dadu Panth Parkhyana" (Recognizing the Dadu Path), it is written:

_lokvedka marag taje | manme ek niranjan bhaje |
isht na rakhe das avatar | dadu panthi so niradhar ||20||_ (One who abandons the worldly-Vedic path and worships in the mind the one stainless Lord, and who does not hold the ten avatars as his chosen deity — know for certain that he is a follower of the Dadu path.)

Those who abandon the path of worldly custom and Vedic ritual, and who inwardly hold devotion to the maya-free Parbrahma, and who do not accept the ten avatars as their object of worship — know for certain that such people are followers of the Dadu path. Thus, besides ourselves, the followers of the Dadu path too are in agreement with our view.

_amrikh gohare aaviyo | sundar shyam swarup ||
so nand dware jivana | je dashrath kul badbhup ||22||_ (He who came at Amrikh's [Ambarish's] cry for help, of beautiful dark-hued form — that same one, O Jivana, plays at Nand's door, he who was the great king of Dashrath's lineage.)

Prabodh (chapter):

Jivandasji Maharaj says: the God of beautiful dark-hued form who came at King Ambarish's cry for protection is the very same God who is now sporting in Nandji's courtyard — he who was the great king in the lineage of King Dashrath.

_amrish gohare aaviyo | hari dharmo natvar vesh ||
sab jag bhulyo jivana | karat anek anek ||23||_ (Hari came at Amrish's [Ambarish's] cry for help, wearing the guise of a master performer. The whole world was deceived, O Jivana, seeing him take on so many, many forms.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says: God, coming to help King Ambarish, took on the guises of the ten avatars like an actor; because of this, the whole world keeps saying that God is many different beings.

Thus, because of the dazzling illusion of the ten avatars, people fail to grasp the true understanding of God as Ram-Krishna, and so, in the matter of devotion to God, the ten avatars have become like a shahukar chor (respectable thief).

God has 24 principal avatars, of which ten are the main ones: 1. Matsya (fish), 2. Kachchha (tortoise), 3. Varah (boar), 4. Nrusinh (man-lion), 5. Vaman (dwarf), 6. Parashuram, 7. Ram, 8. Krishna, 9. Buddha, 10. Kalki. In the Bhagavat, 22 avatars are listed, in which three avatars — Mohini, Hans, and Hayagriv — are excluded [from that count]; within it, Dhanvantari is counted together with [avatars] 12–13. So here we have called only the ten avatars a shahukar chor, because they are the principal ones. But regarding avatars in general, we do not accept the other avatars either. As for Ram and Krishna, we do not accept them merely as avatar-holders, but accept them as the complete Parbrahma, the Supreme God.

Gnaniji Maharaj writes in the Anahar Anga (chapter):

_pure dharki vanagi | gnani das avatar ||
gnani dhyani muni thako | ved na pave paar ||1||_ (The ten avatars are, O wise one, but a sample of the complete essence. Even wise sages, meditators, and munis have grown weary, and even the Vedas cannot reach its far shore.)

Gnaniji Maharaj says: God's ten avatars are but a kind of sample or fragment of His complete Parbrahma essence. Even great sages (jnanis), yogis who meditate through the path of yoga, and munis have grown weary from trying again and again to gain knowledge of it, and even the Vedas have not been able to know it.

_dariya rupi ram hai | lahar ve avatar |
aadi ant madhya nahi | taka eh vistar ||2||_ (Ram is like the ocean, and the avatars are its waves. This expanse of his has no beginning, middle, or end.)

Gnaniji Maharaj says: God's original, true form is as vast as the ocean, and these avatars of his are merely fragments, like the waves that arise in the ocean. This God-essence has no beginning, middle, or end — and it is from that same God that this expanse, in the form of avatars and in the form of the world, has spread out.

Kabirji has said in the Agadh Anga (chapter):

_kabir dariya rupi ram hai | tarang ve avatar |
dou tarang bich agla | take yah vistar ||8||_ (Kabir says: Ram is like the ocean, and the avatars are its waves; wave following wave, one after another ahead — such is his expanse.)

Das Kabirji says: God's original form is as vast as the ocean, and these avatars are like its waves — just as after two waves rise, a further wave follows, and after that wave another wave arises, in that same way these avatars occur one after another.

At the end of the chapter on "Pret Bhojan" (feeding of ghosts) and the unrighteous devotee, in this sakhi of Kabirji, at the end of the hymn (pad) "Santo Aave Jaaye So Maaya," it is written: _das avatar ishwari maya, taku karta kar bujha_ (the ten avatars are God's maya; understand who its doer/creator is). Thus, worldly people have given great importance to the ten avatars, but in the satsang it has been said that these ten avatars are themselves divine maya.

The ten avatars have made a deep impression on the popular mind. An arati (devotional hymn) has even been composed for them — "Jai Vaikunthadhish..." — and in the Geet Govind, Jaidev has described the ten avatars in verse 1.2.1, which has been placed here as a shlok. In Handwritten Manuscript No. 81, page 66, in the hymn (pad) beginning "Pratham Narayan Machharup Avatariya" ("First, Narayan descended in the form of a fish"), the ten avatars are described.
